title: Everything so far, on one line of text

prereqs.why: Two answers come back through reference parameters, and the vector of words goes in through a const one.
Each word is a `std::string` whose characters are examined one at a time.
The words are collected into a vector before anything is asked of them.

statement:
The last of these, and it uses all of it. Write two functions:

```cpp
bool isLetter(char c);

void summarise(const std::vector<std::string>& words,
               int& letters, std::string& longest);
```

- `isLetter` is true for `a`–`z` and `A`–`Z`, and false for
  everything else.
- `summarise` sets `letters` to the total number of letters across
  all the words, and `longest` to the longest word — the first of
  them if several tie.

Read whitespace-separated words until the input runs out, collect
them, and report:

```
input:   the quick brown fox!

output:  words 4
         letters 16
         longest quick
```

`fox!` is four characters and three letters, which is why `letters`
is 16 rather than 17. `quick` and `brown` are both five characters;
`quick` came first.

With no words at all:

```
words 0
letters 0
longest none
```

### The point of the problem

Nothing new. A predicate function, a vector of strings, a nested
loop over the characters of each word, a `const&` input and two
reference outputs — each of which you have now written on its own.
The exercise is putting them together without the program turning
into a single long `main`.

A shape worth copying:

```
main        read the words into a vector; handle the empty case;
            call summarise; print
  summarise walk the words, totalling letters and tracking the
            longest
    isLetter  answer one question about one character
```

Note that `longest` is **not** about letters — it is the longest
word by total characters, punctuation included. Two different
notions of length in one function, which is exactly the sort of
thing a statement has to pin down and a reader has to read
carefully.

### Constraints

Each word is at most 40 characters and there are at most 1000 of
them. Words contain printable ASCII only.

### Boundary cases

- **No words**, or only whitespace: the three lines above, and
  `summarise` is not called.
- **A word with no letters at all**, such as `123`, counts as a
  word, contributes nothing to `letters`, and can still be the
  longest.
- **A tie on length** reports the first, so `cat dog` gives `cat`.
- **Mixed case** counts both: `AbC` is three letters.

### What the grader checks

Submitting runs your program on the cases above and on hidden
ones, and then compiles it a second time with a `main` of this
exercise’s own that calls both functions directly:
`isLetter` on characters just either side of both ranges, and
`summarise` on four vectors, reading `letters` and `longest` back
**after** each call. Before each call `letters` holds something other
than zero — so a `summarise` that adds to it rather than setting it,
or that prints the report itself instead of writing through its
references, comes out wrong even though the program’s own output is
right. Writing the two character ranges inline instead of writing
`isLetter` does not compile against that harness.
hints: Write `isLetter` first and nothing else. It is one `return` with two ranges joined by `||`, and the rest of the program is easier to think about once it exists.

`summarise` has two jobs and one loop: for each word, add its letters to the running count, and replace `longest` if this word is longer. Counting letters needs an inner loop over the word’s characters.
Use `>` rather than `>=` when comparing lengths, or a later word of the same length replaces the one that should have been kept. And remember `longest` is by characters, not by letters.
